newsitem.title: PERU: Sniper fire jolts nervy peace at Peru siege site.
newsitem.headline: Sniper fire jolts nervy peace at Peru siege site.

text.p: A suspected sniper fired three shots outside the besieged Japanese ambassador's home in Lima on Tuesday, rattling nerves as Marxist rebels held 74 hostages for the 28th day in a standoff with the Peruvian government.
The bullets whizzed over the heads of reporters on the roof of a neighbouring house overlooking the diplomatic residence and disappeared into the darkness.
It was not clear who fired the shots, which unlike previous instances of gunfire at the site seemed to come from outside the compound.
"Each one sounded like a low thud as if they came from a silenced gun. They passed over so close I could hear them sizzling," said Gregg Newton, a Reuters photographer.
Cameramen camped out on the roof said the first shot was fired as they stood up to change places. They dived down and lay flat on the roof as two more shots flew above at 20-second intervals.

"Our delegate at the residence did not hear anything in the early morning," said Cecilia Baux, a spokeswoman for the International Committee of the Red Cross. "We do not know where they came from. The situation is totally calm."
Behind security lines two blocks away from the residence, policemen said they did not hear the shots. There were no reports of injuries.
On Monday, the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels fired three bursts of gunfire into the air when a helicopter overflying the residence came too close.

The rebels, who stormed on Dec. 17 a lavish reception at the residence and took hundreds of guests hostage, are armed with assault rifles and grenades and have booby-trapped and mined the diplomatic compound against a surprise attack.
The shots on Tuesday added to the tension as President Alberto Fujimori has refused to rule out using force while talks to end the crisis are at a standstill.

But underlining his determination to show that Peru is carrying on normally despite the siege, Fujimori travelled to the highland county of Ayacucho and played host to visiting Ecuadorean President Abdala Bucaram.
Accompanied by four of his ministers and his close friend Bishop Juan Luis Cipriani, who is helping mediate the crisis, Fujimori left Lima for the first time since the crisis began.
The rebels were waiting to answer the government's proposal that a "guarantor commission" -- including Cipriani -- oversee fresh talks between the deadlocked sides.
The guerrillas placed a sign up to a window in the diplomatic mansion on Monday calling for local television to be allowed into the residence to broadcast their reply.
But government negotiator, Education Minister Domingo Palermo, told reporters he believed the television station did not want to be "a channel of communication for the MRTA."

The negotiations have bogged down in uncompromising positions. The guerrillas have refused to back down on their demand that some 400 jailed MRTA comrades be freed. The government has flatly rejected the demand.

The two sides cancelled a much-anticipated meeting scheduled for Sunday between the rebel leader, Nestor Cerpa Cartolini, and Palermo because the rebels insisted the talks be centred on the release of imprisoned MRTA members.
Palermo, who blames the MRTA for scuppering the latest talks, has proposed the two sides meet under the supervision of the Red Cross and the Vatican's representative, Cipriani.

Fujimori has repeatedly said he will not give in to the guerrillas' demands, dismissing them as "terrorist blackmail." But he has floated the possibility of transporting the rebels to another country if they lay down their arms and release all of their captives.

"Our position and attitude is not to give in to their threat but to leave open the possibility of a peaceful end. The international community has supported this position," state news agency Andina quoted Fujimori as saying during a dinner on Monday with Bucaram.
The MRTA has released most of the more than 500 hostages they seized in what they called "goodwill gestures."

It hopes to use those who remain -- including dozens of Peruvian government and security force officials, the younger brother of Fujimori and Japanese businessmen and diplomats -- as bargaining chips to secure their demand.
